clinical: Arterioles are the main resistance vessels, so sustained constriction of their smooth muscle raises peripheral resistance and blood pressure. Many blood pressure drugs work by relaxing arteriolar smooth muscle.

Capillary network.description: The capillary bed lies between arterioles and venules. Blood enters from an arteriole through a metarteriole, then passes through true capillaries (opened and closed by precapillary sphincters) or the thoroughfare channel, and drains into a venule.
clinical: High blood sugar thickens the basement membrane of capillaries, contributing to small-vessel complications such as retinopathy and nephropathy.
During inflammation, white blood cells leave the bloodstream mainly through postcapillary venules, and fluid leaking from these venules causes the oedema seen in inflamed tissue.
A glomus tumour grows from a glomus body, a shunt-like structure in the skin, and typically causes intense, sharp pain, often under a fingernail. Surgical removal is the usual treatment.

Lymphatics.description: Lymphatic capillaries start blind-ended in the tissues and take up excess interstitial fluid, which becomes lymph. Lymph flows through valved collecting vessels toward lymph nodes and returns to the blood near the base of the neck.
clinical: Blocked or damaged lymph vessels, for example after lymph node removal in breast cancer surgery, lead to lymphoedema, a build-up of protein-rich fluid that swells the tissue.
In sickle cell disease, red cells become stiff and sickle-shaped, and they can jam capillaries and other small vessels, causing pain and tissue damage.

Connective tissue.description: Loose connective tissue surrounds the capillaries and supports them. It contains fibroblasts that make collagen and ground substance, macrophages that clear debris and pathogens, and pericytes that wrap the capillary wall. Collagen fibres give the tissue its strength, and lymphatic capillaries are anchored to them.
clinical: Vitamin C is needed to make stable collagen, so deficiency (scurvy) weakens connective tissue and makes capillaries fragile, causing bleeding into the skin and gums.

Capillary types (3x).description: The three capillary types differ in how leaky they are. Continuous capillaries have a complete endothelium with no pores, fenestrated capillaries have pores (as in kidney glomeruli and intestinal villi), and sinusoidal capillaries are wide and leaky, with gaps between cells and an incomplete basement membrane (as in liver, spleen and bone marrow).
clinical: Continuous capillaries in the brain have tight junctions and astrocyte support, forming the blood-brain barrier, which keeps many drugs and large molecules out of the brain.

parts.description: The tunica intima is the innermost coat of an arteriole, made of a single layer of flattened endothelial cells resting on a thin basement membrane. Blood touches this smooth lining directly, and the endothelium releases chemical messengers such as nitric oxide that help control the diameter of the vessel. Its flat, oval nuclei bulge slightly into the lumen, and outside it lies the wavy internal elastic membrane, which separates the intima from the muscle coat.

The tunica media is the middle coat of an arteriole, made of circularly arranged smooth muscle cells that lie between the internal elastic membrane and the outer coat. Contraction narrows the lumen and relaxation widens it, so this layer is the main controller of the arteriole's resistance and of how much blood enters the capillary network. In a section, look for the elongated muscle nuclei running around the vessel in rings.

The tunica externa is the outermost coat of an arteriole, a thin sheath of loose connective tissue containing collagen and elastic fibres, fibroblasts and small nerve fibres. It surrounds the smooth muscle of the tunica media and anchors the arteriole to the tissue around it. In a section it appears as a pale, fibrous rim outside the muscle layer, and it often merges with the surrounding connective tissue.

The metarteriole is a short vessel that carries blood from an arteriole into the true capillary bed. Its wall is endothelium with only scattered smooth muscle cells outside it, so the muscle does not form the continuous coat seen in an arteriole. Where true capillaries leave it, rings of smooth muscle called precapillary sphincters control how much blood enters them. In a section, look for a small vessel with a thin, interrupted muscle layer, which runs on directly as the thoroughfare channel to a venule.

Metarteriole smooth muscle cells are the individual muscle cells scattered along the wall of a metarteriole, the short vessel that runs between an arteriole and the true capillaries. Unlike the continuous muscle coat of an arteriole, they form a discontinuous layer with gaps between cells, so the wall is only partly surrounded by muscle. In a section, look for isolated, spindle-shaped muscle nuclei set at intervals along the vessel; these cells help regulate the flow of blood into the capillary bed.

Arterial capillaries are the arterial end of the true capillary bed, where blood arrives from a metarteriole. Each capillary is only about 5–10 µm across, so its wall is just a layer of endothelial cells on a basement membrane, with pericytes lying against its outer surface, and red blood cells must pass through in single file. Blood pressure is higher than the osmotic pull of the plasma proteins at this end, so fluid tends to leave the vessel and enter the tissues.

Venous capillaries are the venous end of the true capillary bed, where blood drains on into a venule. Here the hydrostatic pressure has fallen, so the osmotic pull of the plasma proteins draws most of the fluid that left at the arterial end back into the blood, and the rest is drained by lymphatic capillaries. Their wall is the same thin layer of endothelium and basement membrane as the arterial capillaries, so the two ends can only be told apart by their position in the bed.

The thoroughfare channel is the direct continuation of a metarteriole into a venule, a route that bypasses the true capillaries. Blood flows through it continuously, because the precapillary sphincters guard only the side branches that feed the true capillaries, so the channel stays open when those sphincters close. In a section it is a short, fairly straight vessel with sparse smooth muscle, lying between the capillary bed and the venule.

A venule is a small vessel that collects blood from the capillary network and carries it toward the small veins. Its wall is thin and mainly endothelium on a basement membrane, with pericytes in the smallest venules and a few smooth muscle cells in the larger ones, and the number of muscle cells increases as the venule gets wider. In a section, a venule is recognised by its thin wall and a lumen wider than that of the capillaries it drains.

Venule smooth muscle cells are the few muscle cells lying in the wall of a venule, outside the endothelium and basement membrane. They are scarce in the smallest venules, where pericytes take their place, and become more numerous in the larger collecting venules, where they form a thin, incomplete circular layer. Because the muscle is so sparse, venules are easily stretched and can change their diameter far less than arterioles can.

The endothelium of an arteriovenous (AV) anastomosis is the single layer of flattened endothelial cells that lines the short, direct channel joining an arteriole to a venule. It is continuous with the lining of both vessels, so blood passes straight from the arterial side to the venous side without entering the capillary bed. In a section, look for this thin, flat lining inside the thick muscular wall that surrounds the shunt.

The smooth muscle of a glomus is the thick, specialised muscle layer around an arteriovenous anastomosis, the short shunt that carries blood from an arteriole straight into a venule and bypasses the capillaries. Its muscle cells, called glomus cells, are rounded and epithelium-like, packed in concentric layers around a narrow channel. Sympathetic nerves make the muscle contract to close the shunt, which keeps heat in, and relax to open it; glomus bodies are abundant in the skin of the fingertips, nail beds, palms and soles.

Anchoring filaments are fine fibrils that attach the outer surface of a lymphatic capillary to the surrounding collagen and elastic fibres of the connective tissue. When tissue fluid builds up and the tissue swells, these filaments are pulled taut, which holds the capillary open and lets more fluid enter it. Because they are very fine, they are seen as thin threads radiating from the capillary wall mainly under the electron microscope.

A collecting lymphatic vessel is a larger lymph channel formed when lymphatic capillaries join together, and it carries lymph away from the tissues toward the lymph nodes, then on to the lymph trunks and ducts. Its wall has three coats, like a small vein, with a layer of smooth muscle, and it contains one-way valves that divide it into segments that contract to push lymph onward. In a section, look for these valves and a wall with a more developed muscle layer than the lymphatic capillaries have.

A lymphatic vessel valve is a pair of thin, bicuspid flaps, meaning two leaflets, set across the inside of a collecting lymphatic vessel. The leaflets close when lymph tries to flow backwards, so lymph can only move forward, and the valves divide the vessel into short segments that each act as a pump. In a section, look for paired inward folds of the lining, which are most easily seen in the larger collecting vessels.

Lymphocytes in the lymph are small white blood cells, mostly T lymphocytes with some B lymphocytes, that travel in the lymph from the tissues to the lymph nodes. Each has a large, rounded, darkly stained nucleus with only a thin rim of pale cytoplasm, so in a section they look like small, deeply stained cells with little visible cytoplasm. They are part of the body's immune defence, and many recirculate between blood, lymph and the nodes, where they meet antigens.

Red blood cells (erythrocytes) are biconcave discs, about 7.5 µm across, that have no nucleus and carry oxygen bound to haemoglobin. Their flexible membrane lets them deform, bending and squeezing, as they pass through vessels of very different calibre, from narrow capillaries to wider venules. In a section they appear as small, round, bright red profiles, and their lack of a nucleus distinguishes them from other cells.

Pericytes (pericapillary cells) are flattened, branching cells that lie outside the endothelium of capillaries and venules, embedded in their basement membrane. Their long processes wrap around the vessel wall, and they contain contractile proteins such as actin, so they help regulate capillary diameter and stabilise the vessel wall. In a section, a pericyte is recognised by an elongated nucleus that bulges along the outside of a small vessel.

Fibroblasts are the main cells of loose connective tissue, scattered through the tissue around the capillaries. They are spindle-shaped with long, pale cytoplasm, and they make collagen, elastic fibres and ground substance, which give the tissue its strength and elasticity. In a haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) section, look for elongated, pale oval nuclei lying among the collagen fibres.

Macrophages are large phagocytic cells of the connective tissue, derived from blood monocytes, that engulf dead cells, debris and invading bacteria. They are round or irregular in shape, with granular or vacuolated cytoplasm, and they also present antigens to lymphocytes, helping start the immune response. In a haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) section, look for a cell with foamy cytoplasm and a nucleus that is often indented.

Collagen fibres are the thick, strong fibres of the connective tissue around the capillaries, made mainly of type I collagen and secreted by fibroblasts. They are bundles of fibrils, arranged in wavy, interlacing patterns that resist being pulled apart and give the tissue its tensile strength. In haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections they appear as pale pink, undulating bands between the cells, and they are the sites where the anchoring filaments of lymphatic capillaries attach.

The cell nuclei in loose connective tissue belong to its resident cells, mainly fibroblasts and macrophages, with occasional fat cells and mast cells. Fibroblast nuclei are elongated, oval and pale, lying between the collagen bundles, whereas macrophage nuclei tend to be rounder, more compact and often indented. In haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections, comparing nuclear shape is one of the most useful ways to tell these cell types apart.

The endothelial cells of a continuous capillary form an unbroken lining around the lumen, and neighbouring cells are joined by tight junctions near the blood side of the narrow clefts between them. Having no fenestrae, these cells are the least permeable of the capillary types, so lipid-soluble substances cross through the cytoplasm of the cells, while small water-soluble molecules can pass through the clefts. Continuous capillaries are found in muscle, nervous tissue, skin and lungs, and in the brain they form the blood-brain barrier.

The cell junctions of a continuous capillary are tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) that seal the edges of neighbouring endothelial cells. They are built from transmembrane proteins such as claudins and occludin, which join the outer leaflets of the two cell membranes, so the cells form a tight seal rather than a loose join. In an electron micrograph they appear as dense contact points where the membranes of the two cells meet.

The basement membrane of a continuous capillary is a thin, unbroken sheet of extracellular matrix that lies between the endothelial cells and the surrounding tissue. It is made of type IV collagen, laminin and heparan sulphate proteoglycan, and it supports the endothelium while the pericytes sit within it. With periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining, it shows as a continuous magenta outline around each capillary.

A pericyte is a flattened, branching cell that lies embedded within the basement membrane of a continuous capillary, with its processes reaching around the endothelial cells. Its processes meet the endothelium at peg-and-socket junctions, which help hold the two cells together and stabilise the capillary wall. In a section, a pericyte is recognised by its elongated nucleus, which lies outside the endothelium but inside the basement membrane.

A fenestrated capillary has very thin endothelial cells perforated by fenestrae, small pores where the cytoplasm is absent and only a thin membrane, often closed by a fine diaphragm, separates the blood from the tissue. Because of these pores it is highly permeable to water and small solutes, and it is found in the intestinal villi, the choroid plexus, the ciliary processes of the eye and the renal glomeruli. In a section, look for the thin, flattened endothelium with nuclei bulging into the lumen.

The junctions of a fenestrated capillary hold the edges of neighbouring endothelial cells together, so the endothelium forms a continuous lining around the lumen. Most substances cross this capillary through the fenestrae in the cell bodies rather than between the cells, so the junctions are not the main route of exchange. In an electron micrograph they appear as narrow, dark seams between the cells.

The basement membrane of a fenestrated capillary is a continuous sheet of extracellular matrix lying beneath the fenestrated endothelium, and it helps control which molecules can pass. In renal glomerular capillaries it is especially thick and is the main barrier that keeps large plasma proteins in the blood. In an electron micrograph it appears as a continuous, electron-dense layer under the fenestrated endothelium.

Sinusoidal capillaries are wide, irregular capillaries found in the liver, spleen, bone marrow and endocrine glands, where blood flows slowly past the surrounding cells. Their endothelial cells are thin and fenestrated and are separated by wide gaps, so large molecules and whole blood cells can move between the blood and the surrounding tissue. In a section, look for a large, irregular lumen lined by flattened endothelial nuclei.

The basement membrane of a sinusoidal capillary is discontinuous, present only as incomplete patches around the vessel rather than as a continuous sheet. Because of this, plasma and blood cells can reach the surrounding parenchymal cells, such as liver cells (hepatocytes), with little barrier in between. In a section, a sinusoid therefore lacks the complete outline seen around most other capillaries.

Sinusoidal macrophages are fixed macrophages that line the sinusoids, where they remove debris, dead cells and microorganisms from the slow-moving blood. In the liver these cells are called Kupffer cells, and they protect the body from bacteria and endotoxin that reach the liver from the gut in the portal blood. In a section, look for a macrophage on the blood side of the sinusoid lining, with its nucleus bulging into the vessel.

The nuclei in a capillary wall belong mainly to the endothelial cells, which are thin and flattened, so their nuclei bulge into the lumen. Pericyte nuclei are elongated and lie outside the endothelium within the basement membrane, while macrophage nuclei are rounder and often indented. In a section, these nuclei appear as dark, oval or elongated shapes around the lumen, and their position helps identify which cell type each one belongs to.

Red blood cells are biconcave discs with no nucleus that carry oxygen bound to haemoglobin. In narrow continuous and fenestrated capillaries they pass one at a time, deforming their discs so that each fits through the lumen. In a sinusoid the lumen is much wider, so the cells drift through loosely with room to spare. In a section, their lack of a nucleus and strong eosin staining identify them.
